title: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: before a hard lesson, teacher and student say one thing together
carry: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad
tomorrow: why say peace three times, and not just once?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayam atma brahma ended its week in honey: everything feeds and is fed. The four great sayings are done. Now, the chants that stand around the texts.

Teach a sibling to drive, or help a kid with fractions, and somewhere in the hour a voice gets sharp. One question too many. One answer that stings. Both people walk away a little sore. The Upanishads saw that coming. Before a single line of a hard text is opened, teacher and student say a few lines together, in one breath, as equals. Not a warm-up. A prayer for both of them. That's a peace chant.
screen: `A VOICE GETS SHARP.` → `BEFORE THE TEXT OPENS.` → `A PRAYER FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Tradition sets a peace chant at the start and the end of the study of each Upanishad, and each closes the same way: Om, shanti, shanti, shanti. Peace, peace, peace. The next days go through them, and through the lines some Upanishads end on. Today's chant is known by its first words, saha navavatu. The Taittiriya Upanishad puts it at the head of one of its sections, and tradition chants it with the Katha too. Here's what it asks, in plain words. May it protect us both. May it nourish us both. May we work together with strength. May our study be full of light. May we not turn against each other. Notice the word both. The teacher doesn't stand outside the prayer, handing it down. The teacher needs protecting and feeding too. And notice the last request. Of everything that could go wrong in a hard lesson, the chant names this one: that the two people in the room would come to resent each other. Study can do that. A question pushes, an answer stings, and a little bitterness creeps in. So before the text even opens, the chant asks for what the text can't supply: two people still on the same side when the lesson ends.
screen: `EACH UPANISHAD, OPENED WITH PEACE.` · `SAHA NAVAVATU: US BOTH.` · `STRENGTH, AND STUDY FULL OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `MAY WE NOT TURN AGAINST EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: If there's paper nearby, write the name of someone you learn from, and next to it, on the same line, someone who learns from you. Look at the two names side by side for the rest of the sit. If you chant, you can say saha navavatu softly over them.
The peace chants: lines said before and after the study of an Upanishad, each ending in shanti, peace, three times. Saha navavatu asks for teacher and student both.
Pocket this: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad, teacher and student under one prayer. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: your study group is about to start a brutal problem set, and last time it ended in a fight. by saha navavatu, what comes first?
